cs50:1.1.startWhen: Revisit only CS50's Python material during Python Setup and Fundamentals in Phase 01, after the topic's first syntax lessons.
cs50:1.1.whyAtThisStage: The Python week supplies a second worked explanation of the program constructs you are now practicing, without requiring the full course.
cs50:1.1.practicalTask: Trace a short Python loop from the lecture, then adapt it to validate and summarize three student marks.
learningObjectives: Predict a loop result before running it
Explain how a list or dictionary organizes the marks
completionCriteria: The summary handles an empty list and invalid input
Explain the revised code without copying the lecture

ostep:9.5.startWhen: Revisit the Distributed Systems chapter during Phase 09 Distributed Systems, after operating-system basics and queues.
ostep:9.5.whyAtThisStage: The book moves beyond one machine to explain why a remote call can fail ambiguously; it is a foundation, not a complete cloud reliability recipe.
ostep:9.5.practicalTask: Draw a remote request with a delayed or lost reply and explain why the caller cannot infer whether the operation completed. Relate this to an idempotent document job.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a local process failure from a lost message
Explain an ambiguous RPC outcome
completionCriteria: The timeline includes sender, receiver and missing acknowledgement
Document the retry decision and remaining uncertainty

ostep:9.6.startWhen: Return to the concurrency chapters during Concurrency and Performance in Phase 09, after distributed failure fundamentals.
ostep:9.6.whyAtThisStage: Thread interleavings, synchronization and event loops explain the behavior you must measure before increasing worker counts.
ostep:9.6.practicalTask: Trace two interleavings of a shared-counter example, then explain one lock-based fix and one condition-variable use. Connect the result to a bounded worker design.
learningObjectives: Identify a race and its shared state
Explain why more threads need not improve throughput
completionCriteria: Show a failing interleaving and a corrected invariant
Record the assumptions behind the worker limit

maths:2.2.startWhen: Open the counting and set material while studying Discrete Mathematics and Logic in Phase 02, after Basic Mathematics.
maths:2.2.whyAtThisStage: Counting small cases and visualizing set intersections supports this topic; Khan Academy is supplementary to the roadmap's proof and graph lessons.
maths:2.2.practicalTask: Count possible student-course assignments in a tiny example and verify the answer by listing cases. Draw a Venn diagram for two course groups.
learningObjectives: Distinguish permutations from combinations
Interpret a set intersection in an application
completionCriteria: Enumerated and calculated counts agree
State which proof or graph concept still needs the roadmap lesson

maths:2.4.startWhen: Open the probability units during Probability in Phase 02 after descriptive statistics.
maths:2.4.whyAtThisStage: Worked event diagrams make conditional probability interpretable before a statistics API is used.
maths:2.4.practicalTask: Calculate a conditional probability using a small frequency table, then simulate repeated trials to check the scale of the result.
learningObjectives: Distinguish independence from conditional probability
Interpret the denominator in a conditional event
completionCriteria: The frequency table and calculation agree
Explain simulation variation rather than expecting exact equality

maths:2.6.startWhen: Return to selected calculus units during Calculus and Optimization in Phase 02 after functions and linear algebra.
maths:2.6.whyAtThisStage: Derivatives explain how a small parameter change affects a loss; arithmetic revision alone no longer addresses the learning need.
maths:2.6.practicalTask: Differentiate a one-variable squared-error function, check a finite-difference estimate, and show one gradient-descent update.
learningObjectives: Interpret a derivative as local change
Relate a gradient step to a loss value
completionCriteria: The analytic and numerical derivatives approximately agree
State the step size and a case where a large step fails

focusSections: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter
builders:9.3.startWhen: Read overload and retry guidance during Rate Limiting in Phase 09, after caching and basic system design.
builders:9.3.whyAtThisStage: A client that retries too aggressively can defeat a server's capacity plan; these articles complement the limiter implementation.
builders:9.3.practicalTask: Write a client retry policy for a 429 response with a total attempt budget and jitter, then show how it interacts with a token-bucket limit.
learningObjectives: Explain retry amplification
Choose a bounded overload response
completionCriteria: A timeline shows the retry and stop conditions
The policy respects the server's retry signal without an unbounded loop

focusSections: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
builders:9.4.startWhen: Read the idempotency and queue-backlog articles while building a durable job in Phase 09 Queues and Background Processing.
builders:9.4.whyAtThisStage: A queued task may be delivered more than once, and a growing backlog is an operational failure even if requests are accepted.
builders:9.4.practicalTask: Design an idempotency record and bounded retry/dead-letter policy for document ingestion; simulate a duplicate delivery on paper or locally.
learningObjectives: Separate delivery attempts from one logical operation
Recognize backlog growth and recovery limits
completionCriteria: Duplicate deliveries resolve to one logical document
The policy includes a retry limit and observable failure state

focusSections: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter
builders:9.5.startWhen: Revisit remote-failure and idempotency guidance during Distributed Systems in Phase 09 after queues.
builders:9.5.whyAtThisStage: An ambiguous timeout can trigger a second execution; the articles provide design patterns to apply to the distributed-systems concepts.
builders:9.5.practicalTask: Draw success, lost-reply and repeated-request timelines for one CCAI operation and state the durable identity needed to reconcile them.
learningObjectives: Explain why timeout does not prove non-execution
Keep retry side effects bounded
completionCriteria: Every timeline has a defined final state
Document one consistency or availability trade-off

focusSections: Using load shedding to avoid overload
builders:9.6.startWhen: Read the overload-management articles during Concurrency and Performance in Phase 09 after distributed failure concepts.
builders:9.6.whyAtThisStage: A concurrency setting is useful only with an admission and overload policy; this source supports that policy rather than teaching Python profiling APIs.
builders:9.6.practicalTask: Write a bounded admission policy for a slow dependency and compare expected queue wait under two concurrency limits using measured or explicitly assumed numbers.
learningObjectives: Connect work limits to queueing delay
Explain graceful rejection under overload
completionCriteria: Units and workload assumptions are stated
Separate actual measurements from estimates

builders:9.7.startWhen: Read the scalability and overload articles during Scalable AI Systems in Phase 09 after concurrency and performance.
builders:9.7.whyAtThisStage: Model inference consumes bounded workers and memory; ordinary request scaling advice must be tested against that workload.
builders:9.7.practicalTask: Design bounded inference admission, per-tenant quotas and an overload response for CCAI. Explain how a retry budget prevents an outage cascade.
learningObjectives: Identify the scarce inference resource
Define a safe overload behavior
completionCriteria: The design includes limits and a recovery path
Capacity claims are tied to stated measurements or assumptions

builders:11.1.startWhen: Revisit selected reliability articles during AI System Architecture in Phase 11 after system design and observability.
builders:11.1.whyAtThisStage: A complete CCAI design can now expose the dependency and failure boundaries that an isolated pattern cannot establish.
builders:11.1.practicalTask: Annotate one CCAI request diagram with timeout budgets, isolation boundaries and the signals used to detect failure.
learningObjectives: Map a pattern to a concrete dependency boundary
Explain its operational downside
completionCriteria: Each proposed control has an owner and measurement
The note includes one simpler alternative

builders:11.2.startWhen: Return to failure-handling articles during Intelligent Model Routing in Phase 11 after architecture and evaluation fundamentals.
builders:11.2.whyAtThisStage: Provider fallback is a distributed reliability decision; these articles support fallback policy rather than teaching model-capability ranking.
builders:11.2.practicalTask: Write CCAI fallback rules for a timed-out provider, including remaining latency/token budget and duplicate-accounting protection.
learningObjectives: Separate retry from provider fallback
Preserve a request budget across routing attempts
completionCriteria: The policy stops when its budget is exhausted
A failed attempt cannot charge usage twice

builders:11.4.startWhen: Read availability-focused articles during High Availability and Reliability in Phase 11 after a measured serving baseline.
builders:11.4.whyAtThisStage: The architecture now has real dependencies whose failure and recovery behavior can be rehearsed.
builders:11.4.practicalTask: Plan and run a small owned-service dependency-failure drill, recording detection, fallback and recovery observations.
learningObjectives: Relate an availability goal to a failure boundary
Separate recovery evidence from an availability claim
completionCriteria: Record observed recovery time and affected work
Document one failure the drill did not cover

builders:11.5.startWhen: Return to only the relevant engineering articles during Architecture Trade-offs in Phase 11 after the reliability exercises.
builders:11.5.whyAtThisStage: Examples from operating real services help challenge assumptions, but do not establish that the same architecture fits your workload.
builders:11.5.practicalTask: Write one architecture decision comparing a simple queue-based service with a more distributed design, citing the relevant reliability argument and your own workload evidence.
learningObjectives: Explain a design consequence instead of copying a pattern
State the evidence that would reverse the decision
completionCriteria: The decision contains assumptions, costs and a simpler alternative
A trigger for reevaluating the decision is explicit

pytest:3.1.startWhen: Reopen the fixture and test-organization sections during Software Engineering Fundamentals in Phase 03 after Python Professional Development.
pytest:3.1.whyAtThisStage: Tests provide a behavior boundary for a small refactor; pytest does not replace the topic's requirements or architecture work.
pytest:3.1.practicalTask: Refactor one student-record function behind a small interface while keeping behavior tests green, then add a failure-case fixture.
learningObjectives: Use tests to preserve observable behavior
Isolate a dependency in a fixture
completionCriteria: The tests pass before and after the refactor
A deliberate behavior change makes a relevant assertion fail

pytest:10.3.startWhen: Return to pytest during Software and API Testing in Phase 10 after a working API and AI security fundamentals.
pytest:10.3.whyAtThisStage: You now need contract, permission and dependency-failure checks at real boundaries instead of only isolated function examples.
pytest:10.3.practicalTask: Add valid, invalid, unauthorized and failed-provider API cases with deterministic fixtures, plus one isolated database integration check.
learningObjectives: Distinguish unit and integration boundaries
Assert failure behavior without paid provider calls
completionCriteria: A known authorization regression fails the suite
Tests run independently with no shared fixture state

python:1.2.startWhen: Read the functions and Modules chapters during Functions and Modular Programming in Phase 01 after control flow and collections.
python:1.2.whyAtThisStage: Function contracts and module boundaries let the same student-record behavior be reused and tested.
python:1.2.practicalTask: Split mark validation and aggregation into functions in a module, import them from a small CLI, and exercise positional/default/keyword arguments.
learningObjectives: Explain argument binding and a return contract
Distinguish importing a module from running its CLI
completionCriteria: Invalid marks are handled consistently
The module can be imported without starting interactive input

python:1.3.startWhen: Read the Classes chapter during Object-Oriented Programming in Phase 01 after functions and modules.
python:1.3.whyAtThisStage: The tutorial now explains the object and method behavior needed to model records and interchangeable repositories.
python:1.3.practicalTask: Create Student and StudentRepository objects, compare a file-backed and an in-memory implementation, and test that instance data is not shared accidentally.
learningObjectives: Distinguish class attributes from instance state
Use composition or an interface to replace storage
completionCriteria: Two instances keep independent records
The same caller works with both repository implementations

python:1.4.startWhen: Return to the exception, generator and file-cleanup sections during Advanced Python in Phase 01 after classes.
python:1.4.whyAtThisStage: These selected tutorial sections cover iteration and resource handling; typing and async details need the linked standard-library references.
python:1.4.practicalTask: Write a generator-based JSON-to-CSV transformation with a context-managed file and a custom validation exception. Use the separate asyncio guide only for the topic's later async exercise.
learningObjectives: Explain lazy iteration and resource lifetime
Keep invalid records separate from successful output
completionCriteria: A failing input closes files and produces a controlled error
The generator does not require loading the whole dataset

python:1.5.startWhen: Revisit environments, quality-control and timing examples during Python Professional Development in Phase 01 after Advanced Python.
python:1.5.whyAtThisStage: The language tutorial supplies environment and standard-library context; pytest, formatter and linter setup use their own documentation.
python:1.5.practicalTask: Create an isolated environment for the student app, reproduce its dependency setup and time one function using the documented standard-library approach.
learningObjectives: Separate dependency isolation from source packaging
Measure a function without guessing its bottleneck
completionCriteria: A second local environment can reproduce the run
The timing records input size and method

git:3.1.startWhen: Revisit the collaboration chapters during Software Engineering Fundamentals in Phase 03 after the initial Git and Python project.
git:3.1.whyAtThisStage: A reviewable branch and commit history make a refactor inspectable; the book supports version-control practice rather than requirements design itself.
git:3.1.practicalTask: Put one small student-app refactor on a branch, inspect the diff and write a review note explaining behavior preserved and tests run.
learningObjectives: Keep a coherent change separate from unrelated work
Explain a diff to another reviewer
completionCriteria: The branch contains a focused change and useful commit message
A reviewed diff matches the stated behavior

git:10.7.startWhen: Revisit release identity and workflow sections during DevOps and CI/CD in Phase 10 after local checks and the first cloud deployment.
git:10.7.whyAtThisStage: Git identifies the exact source being built; GitHub Actions documentation supplies the CI YAML and runner behavior.
git:10.7.practicalTask: Tag a local practice release, identify its commit and describe how a CI artifact should retain that identity. Use the separate GitHub Actions resource for the workflow file.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a Git tag from a deployment
Trace an artifact back to reviewed source
completionCriteria: The tag resolves to the expected commit
The release note records tests and a rollback source revision

web:7.1.startWhen: Revisit HTTP and web API reference material during API Engineering in Phase 07 after programming and the networking introduction.
web:7.1.whyAtThisStage: Transport semantics explain a prediction endpoint's observable contract; MDN is the HTTP reference, not the generator of your application schema.
web:7.1.practicalTask: Inspect sample success, validation-error and unauthorized requests and specify methods, statuses and headers for one prediction endpoint.
learningObjectives: Distinguish transport status from response data
Explain an HTTP request/response boundary
completionCriteria: The three cases have justified methods and statuses
An untrusted response is validated before display

postgres:3.3.startWhen: Use the relational and JSON sections as a comparison during NoSQL Fundamentals in Phase 03, after PostgreSQL database engineering.
postgres:3.3.whyAtThisStage: A relational baseline helps you decide whether documents simplify actual queries; PostgreSQL documentation does not teach MongoDB's API.
postgres:3.3.practicalTask: Represent one document-metadata example as normalized rows and as a JSON column, then compare update and integrity requirements with the separate MongoDB exercise.
learningObjectives: Compare relational constraints with document flexibility
Choose a model using concrete query patterns
completionCriteria: Both PostgreSQL examples answer the same sample query
Document which integrity rule each design enforces

focusSections: EXPLAIN as a later query check
postgres:3.5.startWhen: Revisit schema and constraint material during Data Modeling and Storage for AI in Phase 03 after PostgreSQL and data pipelines.
postgres:3.5.whyAtThisStage: Documents, source versions and ownership need a durable relational model before embedding indexes are added.
postgres:3.5.practicalTask: Design users, documents and chunks tables with tenant ownership and source-version references; test a foreign-key failure and a deletion rule.
learningObjectives: Model provenance and ownership as data
Separate relational integrity from vector similarity
completionCriteria: A cross-tenant lookup cannot bypass the ownership filter
Deletion behavior is demonstrated on a local fixture

postgres:7.3.startWhen: Return to transaction and application-interface sections during Backend Architecture in Phase 07 after a working FastAPI route.
postgres:7.3.whyAtThisStage: A repository boundary must preserve database correctness when requests fail; the source supports persistence behavior rather than the whole backend architecture.
postgres:7.3.practicalTask: Implement or sketch one transaction-backed document repository and test a failed multi-step write using the topic's selected Python driver.
learningObjectives: Keep a business operation atomic
Place connection and transaction ownership explicitly
completionCriteria: A failure rolls back the partial write
The test identifies its driver and isolation assumptions

numpy:2.6.startWhen: Use tiny NumPy arrays to check calculations during Calculus and Optimization in Phase 02 after matrix shapes.
numpy:2.6.whyAtThisStage: Vectorized numerical examples can check a derivative estimate, but the derivative and optimization reasoning belong to the mathematics lesson.
numpy:2.6.practicalTask: Evaluate a quadratic loss at nearby parameter values, compare its finite-difference slope with the hand derivative and perform one update.
learningObjectives: Use shapes and reductions consistently
Distinguish a numerical estimate from an analytic derivative
completionCriteria: Hand and numerical slopes approximately agree
The result states epsilon, dtype and step size

sklearn:4.3.startWhen: Read selected supervised-estimator guides during Supervised Learning in Phase 04 after the estimator interface and data preparation.
sklearn:4.3.whyAtThisStage: You can now compare model assumptions instead of merely learning fit and predict syntax.
sklearn:4.3.practicalTask: Compare a linear model, tree and forest on the same split and preprocessing, reporting one relevant held-out metric and error pattern.
learningObjectives: Connect estimator assumptions to a task
Keep model comparisons leakage-free
completionCriteria: All candidates use the same held-out cases
Explain one error pattern and a model trade-off

sklearn:4.4.startWhen: Read clustering and PCA guides during Unsupervised Learning in Phase 04 after the estimator interface and scaling.
sklearn:4.4.whyAtThisStage: Unlabeled structure needs different interpretation from supervised accuracy; cluster IDs are not known semantic labels.
sklearn:4.4.practicalTask: Scale a small dataset, compare K-means and DBSCAN and inspect a PCA projection with clearly stated evaluation limits.
learningObjectives: Interpret clustering without invented ground truth
Explain how scaling affects distances
completionCriteria: Record parameters and a noise/outlier example
Avoid treating cluster numbers as meaningful categories

sklearn:4.5.startWhen: Read the metrics and validation guides during Model Evaluation in Phase 04 after fitting initial models.
sklearn:4.5.whyAtThisStage: A fitted model gives each metric a concrete mistake pattern; this is the point to assess what a headline score hides.
sklearn:4.5.practicalTask: Compute a tiny confusion matrix by hand, check it with scikit-learn and compare two decision thresholds on held-out examples.
learningObjectives: Relate metric changes to false positives and negatives
Keep threshold selection separate from final test evaluation
completionCriteria: Hand and library counts agree
Explain the chosen operating threshold and one subgroup limitation

sklearn:4.6.startWhen: Read pipeline, search and reproducibility guidance during Model Training and Improvement in Phase 04 after evaluation fundamentals.
sklearn:4.6.whyAtThisStage: A controlled search must fit preprocessing only on training folds and preserve the same inference transformations.
sklearn:4.6.practicalTask: Compare a small hyperparameter search with a baseline in a Pipeline, log settings and save the complete trusted inference pipeline.
learningObjectives: Avoid preprocessing leakage during search
Preserve training/inference transformations
completionCriteria: The search space and validation method are recorded
Reloading the trusted artifact reproduces predictions

pytorch:5.3.startWhen: Revisit network modules and architecture examples during Neural Network Architectures in Phase 05 after the first PyTorch training loop.
pytorch:5.3.whyAtThisStage: Tensor operations now support an architectural comparison; repeating only the tensor introduction would not explain the new layer choices.
pytorch:5.3.practicalTask: Compare a tiny fully connected model and CNN on the same small image fixture, tracing shapes and evaluation behavior.
learningObjectives: Trace shapes through different layer types
Separate training mode from evaluation mode
completionCriteria: Inputs and outputs have documented shapes
A measured comparison uses the same fixture and metric

pytorch:5.4.startWhen: Read device and transfer tutorials during GPU and Model Training Fundamentals in Phase 05 after tensor and architecture practice.
pytorch:5.4.whyAtThisStage: Memory placement and transfers explain throughput bottlenecks; compatible hardware is optional for the conceptual work.
pytorch:5.4.practicalTask: Estimate parameter/gradient memory and measure a small available-device workload with synchronized timing, or annotate supplied timings if no GPU is available.
learningObjectives: Separate compute time from data-transfer time
State precision and memory assumptions
completionCriteria: The report identifies actual versus reference-only results
No unsupported speed claim is made without the device and workload

pytorch:6.3.startWhen: Open the attention tutorial during Transformer Architecture in Phase 06 after the topic's attention equations and the PyTorch basics.
pytorch:6.3.whyAtThisStage: Small matrices let you verify the attention operation before adding an entire pretrained model.
pytorch:6.3.practicalTask: Implement a tiny attention calculation and causal mask, then compare valid shapes and one masked output with the reference explanation.
learningObjectives: Connect attention equations to tensor dimensions
Explain why future-token masking matters
completionCriteria: The causal mask blocks the intended positions
The comparison records input shapes and tolerance

huggingface:6.3.startWhen: Read the transformer overview sections during Transformer Architecture in Phase 06 after basic language-model concepts.
huggingface:6.3.whyAtThisStage: The course connects tokenization and pretrained model families to the architecture lesson; the low-level attention exercise uses the PyTorch resource.
huggingface:6.3.practicalTask: Compare encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder use cases and trace token IDs into one selected model's input contract.
learningObjectives: Distinguish transformer families
Explain the tokenizer/model input boundary
completionCriteria: Each family has a justified task example
The trace labels token and hidden-state shapes without claiming to train a full model

huggingface:6.4.startWhen: Revisit inference and tokenization material during LLM Internals in Phase 06 after the transformer overview.
huggingface:6.4.whyAtThisStage: Concrete token inputs and outputs make inference/context behavior inspectable; advanced serving optimization is a later resource.
huggingface:6.4.practicalTask: Trace a short inference example with fixed settings and compare input token count, output length and a documented context limit using a small model or supplied trace.
learningObjectives: Separate tokenization from generation
Interpret a model output without assuming factual correctness
completionCriteria: The model/tokenizer and settings are identified
A context or generation limitation is documented

focusSections: Advanced LLM fine-tuning as a later subset
huggingface:6.5.startWhen: Read the fine-tuning introduction during LLM Training and Adaptation in Phase 06 after LLM Internals and prompt/context design.
huggingface:6.5.whyAtThisStage: A prompt-only baseline gives you something to compare against adaptation; the advanced course chapters are optional extensions.
huggingface:6.5.practicalTask: Prepare a tiny licensed dataset and disjoint evaluation set, then compare a prompt-only baseline with a small adaptation plan or CPU-feasible example.
learningObjectives: Distinguish prompting from weight updates
Prevent evaluation examples from leaking into adaptation
completionCriteria: The data split and license are explicit
The report states cost, overfitting risk and whether training actually ran

huggingface:7.4.startWhen: Revisit only local model/tokenizer interface examples during AI Provider Integration in Phase 07 after the Hugging Face ecosystem topic.
huggingface:7.4.whyAtThisStage: A known input/output contract helps isolate one local adapter; commercial API authentication, retries and provider billing use their own provider guides.
huggingface:7.4.practicalTask: Wrap a tiny local or mocked Hugging Face inference call behind the CCAI adapter interface and normalize its output without exposing implementation details.
learningObjectives: Separate a local model adapter from a hosted-provider API
Normalize an output contract
completionCriteria: The adapter is testable with supplied responses
The note identifies which hosted-provider behaviors this course does not cover

huggingface:7.5.startWhen: Reopen tokenization and truncation sections during Token and Cost Engineering in Phase 07 after provider integration.
huggingface:7.5.whyAtThisStage: The tokenizer supports length estimation; the course is not a current price list or a guarantee of another provider's billing tokenizer.
huggingface:7.5.practicalTask: Count tokens for several inputs with one identified tokenizer, reserve output capacity and compare a truncation policy. Keep provider prices and billing counts separately configurable.
learningObjectives: Explain tokenizer-dependent length
Distinguish estimated usage from billed usage
completionCriteria: The tokenizer and context budget are recorded
The estimate is not presented as an exact unrelated provider charge

huggingface:8.1.startWhen: Read the semantic-search worked example during Embeddings and Vector Search in Phase 08 after linear algebra and model/tokenizer fundamentals.
huggingface:8.1.whyAtThisStage: The course provides an executable embedding/search example; storage, tenant filtering and pgvector operators belong to their respective resources.
huggingface:8.1.practicalTask: Inspect the example's embedding model and pooling, embed a tiny corpus and test two queries with known relevant results.
learningObjectives: Distinguish retrieval embeddings from arbitrary token hidden states
Keep one model and dimension convention
completionCriteria: Record the embedding model and vector shape
Inspect a failed query instead of assuming all embeddings are comparable

focusSections: Semantic search with FAISS worked example
huggingface:8.3.startWhen: Revisit the embedding/search and input-preparation examples while building Traditional RAG in Phase 08 after a vector-search baseline.
huggingface:8.3.whyAtThisStage: This source supports the embedding and context-input parts of RAG; document authorization, vector SQL and evaluation need the other roadmap resources.
huggingface:8.3.practicalTask: Preserve source IDs while preparing a tiny embedding dataset, inspect the retrieved rows for two queries and ensure the chosen context fits the tokenizer budget.
learningObjectives: Keep source identity through preprocessing
Distinguish a retriever result from a supported generated answer
completionCriteria: Retrieved rows can be traced to original sources
The report identifies an unanswerable or missing-evidence case

huggingface:8.4.startWhen: Use the course's search/data-preparation sections as a supporting reference during Advanced RAG in Phase 08, after measuring the basic RAG baseline.
huggingface:8.4.whyAtThisStage: A preprocessing or embedding change can alter retrieval, but this course is not a complete hybrid/reranking architecture manual.
huggingface:8.4.practicalTask: Change one dataset or embedding-preparation choice and compare retrieved source IDs on fixed questions; use the separate pgvector/evaluation guidance for indexed retrieval and answer scores.
learningObjectives: Control one preprocessing change
Explain the source's limits for advanced retrieval design
completionCriteria: The before/after cases and source IDs are retained
No unsupported claim about end-to-end RAG quality is based only on vector similarity

huggingface:11.2.startWhen: Revisit model-family and context-limit material during Intelligent Model Routing in Phase 11 after provider adapters and evaluation.
huggingface:11.2.whyAtThisStage: Model descriptions inform a capability registry, but routing policy, pricing and availability must be measured or configured elsewhere.
huggingface:11.2.practicalTask: Record input limits and task suitability for two candidate models in CCAI's registry, separating documented claims from your own fixed-input evaluation.
learningObjectives: Distinguish declared capability from measured suitability
Keep tokenizer/context assumptions per model
completionCriteria: Every registry claim has a source or labeled measurement
A fallback rule is justified independently of model popularity

huggingface:11.3.startWhen: Use the course only to prepare a reproducible single-model inference baseline during Phase 11 Model Serving and Inference Optimization, before comparing a serving engine.
huggingface:11.3.whyAtThisStage: A stable model/input baseline is required before vLLM, CUDA or Ray changes can be interpreted; engine deployment is outside this course's scope.
huggingface:11.3.practicalTask: Record a small model's fixed input, tokenizer, output and resource assumptions, then use the selected serving-engine resource for one controlled performance comparison.
learningObjectives: Keep model/input identity stable across benchmarks
Separate application baseline work from serving-engine configuration
completionCriteria: The baseline is reproducible or clearly labeled reference-only
The serving comparison names its separate engine documentation

fastapi:7.3.startWhen: Read application-structure and dependency sections during Backend Architecture in Phase 07 after your first FastAPI API and database concepts.
fastapi:7.3.whyAtThisStage: The framework supplies explicit request/dependency lifetimes for a service/repository design; it does not choose the business architecture for you.
fastapi:7.3.practicalTask: Move one prediction endpoint into a router, inject a repository and override it in tests, checking cleanup on a failed request.
learningObjectives: Separate routing from business logic
Explain the lifetime of an injected dependency
completionCriteria: The same route works with a test repository
Failure releases the request-scoped resource

fastapi:7.4.startWhen: Reopen validation, dependency and response-model sections during AI Provider Integration in Phase 07 after backend architecture.
fastapi:7.4.whyAtThisStage: Provider adapters need a validated application boundary; provider role syntax, SDK retries and pricing come from that provider's own documentation.
fastapi:7.4.practicalTask: Inject a mocked provider into a validated route, normalize its response and reject malformed generated data without logging credentials or private prompts.
learningObjectives: Keep provider details behind an interface
Validate untrusted model output at the API boundary
completionCriteria: Valid and malformed mock responses have deterministic tests
A failure returns a controlled error contract

fastapi:7.6.startWhen: Use the error-handling and testing sections during AI Backend Reliability in Phase 07 after provider integration and usage accounting.
fastapi:7.6.whyAtThisStage: FastAPI exposes controlled responses and cleanup; backoff, retry budgets and circuit breakers must be designed separately for the provider client.
fastapi:7.6.practicalTask: Simulate timeout and malformed-provider responses behind a dependency, assert the mapped status/error and verify cleanup. Document the separate bounded retry policy.
learningObjectives: Separate framework error mapping from provider retry policy
Keep resources and usage accounting consistent on failure
completionCriteria: No failed call leaves a request resource open
The test shows controlled errors without retrying indefinitely

redis:9.3.startWhen: Read atomic counter and expiry guidance during Rate Limiting in Phase 09 after the caching/Redis introduction.
redis:9.3.whyAtThisStage: Concurrent requests need an atomic decision, not independent read-then-write counters.
redis:9.3.practicalTask: Implement a small tenant-scoped limiter, test simultaneous calls and expiry, and document the failure policy when Redis is unavailable.
learningObjectives: Preserve an atomic counter/expiry invariant
Explain per-tenant key boundaries
completionCriteria: A concurrent test does not admit excess requests under the chosen rule
Denied requests include a controlled retry signal

docker:10.7.startWhen: Return to build/tag and image-publishing sections during DevOps and CI/CD in Phase 10 after the first container and cloud deployment.
docker:10.7.whyAtThisStage: Docker documentation defines the artifact; GitHub Actions documentation defines the workflow that builds it.
docker:10.7.practicalTask: Build a tagged prediction-API image locally, record its source revision and test startup/health behavior. Draft the CI invocation using the separate Actions guide.
learningObjectives: Separate image creation from CI orchestration
Trace a runtime artifact to source
completionCriteria: The image runs with documented configuration
The source revision and rollback image identity are recorded

mlflow:10.4.startWhen: Open the LLMs and Agents evaluation documentation during AI and LLM Evaluation in Phase 10 after a working LLM application and testing; do not use the traditional model-registry section for this visit.
mlflow:10.4.whyAtThisStage: MLflow can retain LLM traces, evaluation cases and comparisons; lifecycle/registry work belongs to the later MLOps visit.
mlflow:10.4.practicalTask: Record a small fixed document-assistant or CCAI evaluation with input/source/output provenance and one changed version, inspecting failed or disputed scores.
learningObjectives: Distinguish LLM evaluation from traditional model registry
Keep comparison data and scorer settings reproducible
completionCriteria: The two versions use identical cases
A failure trace and scorer limitation are documented

otel:11.1.startWhen: Revisit propagation and instrumentation design during AI System Architecture in Phase 11 after implementing basic observability.
otel:11.1.whyAtThisStage: The architecture now spans several boundaries, so an isolated request log is insufficient to explain a slow or failed flow.
otel:11.1.practicalTask: Annotate a CCAI request diagram with span boundaries, propagation, safe attributes and sampling decisions; identify where private context must be excluded.
learningObjectives: Connect a dependency boundary to a trace
Choose useful low-cardinality attributes
completionCriteria: A request can be followed across the proposed boundaries
The plan excludes secrets and raw private document content

neo4j:8.6.startWhen: Read relationship-query and traversal sections during Graph RAG in Phase 08 after a working vector RAG baseline and graph fundamentals.
neo4j:8.6.whyAtThisStage: The graph database implements relationship retrieval; extraction quality and answer grounding must still be evaluated separately.
neo4j:8.6.practicalTask: Retrieve a bounded provenance-bearing subgraph for a relationship question and compare its evidence with vector-only retrieval on the same question set.
learningObjectives: Bound graph expansion
Preserve provenance in retrieved relationships
completionCriteria: Every returned relationship has a source
The report includes one extraction error and a case where the graph does not help

owasp:10.10.startWhen: Revisit disclosure and data-handling risks during Privacy, Governance, and Responsible AI in Phase 10 after the security topics.
owasp:10.10.whyAtThisStage: OWASP supports engineering controls and threat analysis; current legal applicability must come from the official jurisdiction-specific sources.
owasp:10.10.practicalTask: Review one CCAI data flow for prompt/log disclosure, retention exposure and cross-tenant access, then separate engineering findings from legal questions.
learningObjectives: Map an AI risk to a concrete data boundary
Distinguish a security control from proof of compliance
completionCriteria: The review names a testable mitigation and its limits
No claim of legal compliance relies only on OWASP

ml-course:5.1.startWhen: Read the neural-network modules during Deep Learning Fundamentals in Phase 05 after ML evaluation and model training.
ml-course:5.1.whyAtThisStage: The conceptual course connects earlier loss/gradient ideas to hidden layers; the PyTorch resource supplies implementation details later.
ml-course:5.1.practicalTask: Sketch a tiny network's forward computation and explain how a parameter update could reduce loss, then compare two supplied training/validation curves.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of an activation
Identify overfitting from separate training and validation evidence
completionCriteria: The sketch labels inputs, parameters and output
The curve interpretation proposes a testable regularization change

focusSections: Getting started: vector type and dimensions
pgvector:8.1.startWhen: Use only the vector type and exact-search sections during Embeddings and Vector Search in Phase 08 after the introductory similarity lessons. Defer ANN indexes until Vector Databases.
pgvector:8.1.whyAtThisStage: A small SQL example connects embedding geometry to a durable query without making index tuning a prerequisite for embeddings.
pgvector:8.1.practicalTask: Store a few supplied same-model vectors and compare exact rankings under cosine and inner-product operators, retaining source IDs.
learningObjectives: Keep dimensions and model identity consistent
Interpret a distance operator's ranking
completionCriteria: Document vector provenance and dimensions
One expected relevant result is checked manually

pgvector:8.3.startWhen: Revisit filtering and vector-query sections during Traditional RAG in Phase 08 after an exact/indexed search baseline.
pgvector:8.3.whyAtThisStage: The database must return authorized evidence with provenance; pgvector itself does not generate grounded answers.
pgvector:8.3.practicalTask: Write a tenant-filtered retrieval query that joins chunk/source metadata, then test an allowed query and a denied cross-tenant fixture.
learningObjectives: Combine similarity and ownership constraints
Keep retrieved chunks traceable to sources
completionCriteria: Another tenant's chunks cannot appear
Returned evidence includes source IDs and the query/model version

pgvector:8.4.startWhen: Read index/filter tuning sections during Advanced RAG in Phase 08 only after measuring a working RAG baseline.
pgvector:8.4.whyAtThisStage: Approximate search and metadata filters can change recall; source-level measurements must precede a tuning claim.
pgvector:8.4.practicalTask: Compare exact retrieval with one ANN configuration on fixed labeled queries under the same tenant filter; record recall, latency and query settings.
learningObjectives: Measure recall against an exact baseline
Explain filter/index interactions
completionCriteria: The same authorized cases are used for both runs
The report records index parameters and one failure case

focusSections: Set up a WSL development environment
linux:1.6-bash.startWhen: Consult the WSL environment and interoperability sections while studying Bash in Phase 01, after the command-line setup. This is an environment reference, not a Bash-language manual.
linux:1.6-bash.whyAtThisStage: You need to know where a shell script runs and how paths cross the Windows/Linux boundary; the Bash lessons supply language concepts.
linux:1.6-bash.practicalTask: Run a supplied harmless input-checking script in a temporary WSL directory and document its working directory, interpreter and Windows/Linux path mapping.
learningObjectives: Identify the shell environment and file boundary
Distinguish WSL setup from Bash syntax
completionCriteria: The supplied script runs in the documented environment
Linux/macOS learners can state the equivalent existing-shell setup without installing WSL
